426--- Note to developers:
427---     NOTATION: SAZ 2024: It is important that this custom notation be at a
428---     level higher than 1 when added to the `constr` grammar because it
429---     interacts with the "application" case of `com` and the notation for
430---     Hoare triples. That grammar parses embedded function arguments at level
431---     1. We never want `f {{P}}` to parse `{ P }` as an assertion when used
432---     in a command. Instead we want `{{P}}` to "close" the Hoare triple.
433---
434---     `NOTATION: Note for Rocq custom grammar hackers.  From what I can tell, the
435---     Rocq LL(1) parser does left-factorize the grammar, *however* it uses a very
436---     strict notion of what counts as "equal" for the purposes of the factorization.
437---     In particular, a grammar entry might have a level,
438---     as in [e custom assn at level 99] in the notation below.  Leaving out the
439---     "at level 99" is *semantically equivalent*, because the [assn] grammar starts
440---     at that level, but omitting it will not work because the grammar for
441---     Hoare triples below includes "at level 99" -- the [LEVEL "99"] part of the
442---     grammar counts for factorization.
443---
444---     The upshot is that means that this notation and the Hoare triple notation
445---     (which overlaps with [{{ _ }}]) must be changed in tandem and use identical
446---     level specifications.`

501--- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
502-
503--- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
504--- command. The standard notation is
505-
506---   {P} c {Q}
507-
508--- meaning:
509-
510--- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
511--- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
512--- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
513-
514--- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
515--- *postcondition*.
516-
517--- Because single braces are already used for other things in Lean, we'll
518--- write Hoare triples with double braces:
519-
520---   {{P}} c {{Q}}
521-
522--- For example,
523-
524--- - The Hoare triple
525-
526---   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
527-
528--- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
529--- a state in which `X = 1`.
530-
531--- - On the other hand,
532-
533---   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
534-
535--- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
536--- `{{X = m}} X :=
537--- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
538--- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
539--- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
540-

691-def ValidHoareTriple
692-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=

698--- Note to developers:
699---     `NOTATION: SAZ 2024 One trickiness of these notations is that we
700---     want the [com] and [assn] grammars to be "open", so that they can
701---     include expressions parsed by the full [constr] grammar of Rocq.
702---     However, then there is a conflict of precedence of the
703---     "application" cases:
704---
705---     The example " {{ True }} X := 0 {{ False }} " does not parse as
706---     intended because the [com] grammar includes the capability of
707---     parsing the (ill-typed) term "0 {{ False }}".
708---
709---     This means that the "application" for [com] should disallow
710---     arguments at the level at which the [assn] grammar is included
711---     in constr.  The upshot is that this notation should be included
712---     in the grammar at the *same* level as the assertion notation
713---     [{{ P }}], which is 2.`

784--- ## Proof Rules
785-
786--- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
787--- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
788--- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
789--- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
790--- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
791--- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
792--- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
793--- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
794--- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
795-
796--- ### Skip
797-
798--- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
799-
800---   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
801---   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
802-
803-theorem hoare_skip (P : Assertion) :
804-    {{ P }} skip; {{ P }} := by
805-  intro st st' h hp
806-  inversion h
807-  assumption
808-
809--- ### Sequencing
810-
811--- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
812--- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
813--- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
814--- where `R` holds:
815-
816---    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
817---    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
818---   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
819---   {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
820-
821-theorem hoare_seq (P Q R : Assertion) (c1 c2 : Com)
822-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
823-    {{ P }} ~c1 ~c2 {{ R }} := by
824-  intro st st' h12 pre
825-  inversion h12 with
826-  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
827-    exact h1 _ _ hc2 (h2 _ _ hc1 pre)
828-
829--- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
830--- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
831--- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
832--- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
833--- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
834--- through commands until we reach the beginning.
835-
836--- ### Assignment
837-
838--- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
839--- rules. Here's how it works.
840-
841--- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
842-
843---   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
844-
845--- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
846--- could the precondition be?
847-
848--- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
849--- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
850-
851---   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
852-
853--- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
854--- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
855--- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
856--- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
857--- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
858-
859--- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
860-
861---   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
862-
863--- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
864--- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
865-
866---   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
867-
868--- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
869--- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
870--- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
871--- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
872--- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
873--- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
874--- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
875-
876--- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
877--- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
878--- expression `a`:
879-
880---   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
881-
882--- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
883--- replaced by `a`.
884-
885--- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
886--- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
887-
888--- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
889-
890---   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
891-
892--- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
893--- terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
894--- start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted
895--- for every occurrence of `X`.
896-
897--- To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it proceeds
898--- from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes good sense to
899--- go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is more important,
900--- because it characterizes what will be true after running the code.
901-
902--- Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment rule.
903--- We'll do that later in some exercises.
904-
905--- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
906-
907---   {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
908---     X := X + 1
909---   {{ X ≤ 5 }}
910-
911---   {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
912---     X := 3
913---   {{ X = 3 }}
914-
915---   {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
916---     X := 3
917---   {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
918-
919--- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of "substituting an
920--- expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which we refer to as
921--- assertion substitution, or `Assertion.sub`.
922-
923--- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
924--- expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just the
925--- same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
926-
927--- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions for
928--- Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends). The
929--- difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
930--- directly "edit" its text.
931-
932--- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
933--- state, defined as follows:
934-
935-def Assertion.sub (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
936-  fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
937-
938--- Note to developers (One An @meluge, before next release):
939---     Introduce a notation typeclass for this (e.g. HasSubst)

941-/-- Assertion substitution: `P [X ↦ a]` -/
942-syntax:100 term:100 " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
943-
944-macro_rules
945-  | `($P [$x ↦ $a]) => `(Assertion.sub $x (aexp { $a }) $P)
946-  -- | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a])) => ``(assn($st; $P) [$x ↦ $a]) -- maybe we could push substitutions inside

948--- This notation allows us to write this operation as:
949-
950---   P [ X ↦ a ]
951-
952-#check (fun st => Assertion.sub X (aexp { 2 * X }) ({{ X ≤ 10 }}) st)
953-#check {{ X ≤ 10 }} [X ↦ 2 * X]
954-#check (∀ st, ({{ X ≤ 10 }} [X ↦ 2 * X]) st)
955-
956--- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` -- that
957--- behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the variable `X`
958--- in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the expression `a`.
959-
960--- To see how this works in more detail, let's calculate what happens with a
961--- couple of examples. First, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3]` -- that is,
962--- more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
963-
964---   fun st =>
965---     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
966---     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st 3 ; st),
967-
968--- which simplifies to
969-
970---   fun st =>
971---     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)

581+-- ### Assertion Implication
582+
583+-- Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies* `Q`, written
584+-- `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state `st`, `Q` also holds.
585+
586+def AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
587+  ∀ st, P st → Q st
588+
589+-- Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is analogous to the
590+-- "usual" Lean implication `→`.
591+
592+notation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
593+
594+theorem assertImplies_def {P Q : Assertion} : P ->> Q ↔ ∀ st, P st → Q st := by rfl
595+
596+-- We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between assertions:
597+
598+notation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
599+
600+theorem assertIff_def {P Q : Assertion} : P <<->> Q ↔ AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
601+    := by rfl
602+

604+-- assertions back in `->>` and `<<->>` notation.

616+/-- `<<->>` abbreviates a conjunction of two `AssertImplies`, so its

625+  guard <| l.isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2 && r.isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2
626+  guard <| l.appFn!.appArg! == r.appArg! && l.appArg! == r.appFn!.appArg!

633+-- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
634+
635+-- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
636+-- command. A commond notation for Hoare triples, and the one we use in this
637+-- book, is
638+
639+--   {{P}} c {{Q}}
640+
641+-- meaning:
642+
643+-- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
644+-- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
645+-- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
646+
647+-- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
648+-- *postcondition*.
649+
650+-- For example,
651+
652+-- - The Hoare triple
653+
654+--   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
655+
656+-- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
657+-- a state in which `X = 1`.
658+
659+-- - On the other hand,
660+
661+--   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
662+
663+-- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
664+-- `{{X = m}} X :=
665+-- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
666+-- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
667+-- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
668+
669+-- _Quiz:_
670+
671+-- Paraphrase the following in English.
672+
673+--   1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
674+
675+--   2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
676+
677+--   3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
678+
679+--   4) {{True}} c {{False}}
680+
681+--   5) ∀ m,
682+--        {{X = m}}
683+--        c
684+--        {{Y = real_fact m}}
685+
686+--   6) ∀ m,
687+--        {{X = m}}
688+--        c
689+--        {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
690+
691+-- _Quiz:_
692+
693+-- Is the following Hoare triple *valid* -- i.e., is the claimed relation
694+-- between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
695+
696+--   {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
697+
698+-- (A) Yes
699+
700+-- (B) No
701+
702+-- _Quiz:_
703+
704+-- What about this one?
705+
706+--   {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
707+
708+-- (A) Yes
709+
710+-- (B) No
711+
712+-- _Quiz:_
713+
714+-- What about this one?
715+
716+--   {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
717+
718+-- (A) Yes
719+
720+-- (B) No
721+
722+-- _Quiz:_
723+
724+-- What about this one?
725+
726+--   {{X = 2 ∧ X = 3}} X := 5 {{X = 0}}
727+
728+-- (A) Yes
729+
730+-- (B) No
731+
732+-- _Quiz:_
733+
734+-- What about this one?
735+
736+--   {{True}} skip {{False}}
737+
738+-- (A) Yes
739+
740+-- (B) No
741+
742+-- _Quiz:_
743+
744+-- What about this one?
745+
746+--   {{False}} skip {{True}}
747+
748+-- (A) Yes
749+
750+-- (B) No
751+
752+-- _Quiz:_
753+
754+-- What about this one?
755+
756+--   {{True}} while true do skip end {{False}}
757+
758+-- (A) Yes
759+
760+-- (B) No
761+
762+-- _Quiz:_
763+
764+-- This one?
765+
766+--   {{X = 0}}
767+--     while X = 0 do X := X + 1 end
768+--   {{X = 1}}
769+
770+-- (A) Yes
771+
772+-- (B) No
773+
774+-- _Quiz:_
775+
776+-- This one?
777+
778+--   {{X = 1}}
779+--     while X ≠ 0 do X := X + 1 end
780+--   {{X = 100}}
781+
782+-- (A) Yes
783+
784+-- (B) No

787+
788+-- Which of the following Hoare triples are *valid* -- i.e., the claimed
789+-- relation between `P`, `c`, and `Q` is true?
790+
791+--   1) {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}

798+

800+

802+
803+--   7) {{True}} while true do skip end {{False}}
804+

806+--       while X = 0 do X := X + 1 end

815+-- ## Hoare Triples, Formally
816+
817+-- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
818+
819+open scoped HasEval
820+
821+def ValidHoareTriple
822+    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
823+  ∀ {st st' : State},
824+    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
825+    P st →
826+    Q st'
827+
828+-- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
829+--     Somethings strange is going on in `theorem if_example`, using
830+--     `apply hoare_consequence_pre` followed by `· exact hoare_asgn` works,
831+--     but `refine hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn ?_` or
832+--     `apply hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn` don't. The only solution I
833+--     found was to mark `ValidHoareTriple` irreducible.
834+--
835+--     It has to do something with `apply` and `refine` looking inside the
836+--     implication in `∀ {st st'}, ...`
837+
838+-- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two assertions is
839+-- parsed with the same grammar as the `imp { … }` notation, so a command that
840+-- is a Lean variable (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`,
841+-- just as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.
842+
843+class HasTriple (Com : Type) where
844+  Triple : Assertion → Com → Assertion → Prop
845+
846+namespace HasTriple
847+
848+/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` -/
849+scoped notation:lead "{{" P "}} " c:lead " {{" Q "}}" => Triple ({{ P }}) c ({{ Q }})
850+
851+/-- Hoare triple with `imp_com` command syntax -/
852+scoped syntax:lead (priority := high) "{{" term "}} " imp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
853+scoped macro_rules
854+  | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
855+      ``(HasTriple.Triple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
856+end HasTriple
857+
858+instance : HasTriple Com where
859+  Triple := ValidHoareTriple
860+
861+open scoped HasTriple
862+
863+theorem validHoareTriple_def {P : Assertion} {c : Com} {Q : Assertion} :
864+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} ↔ ∀ {st st' : State},
865+      (st =[ c ]=> st') →
866+      P st →
867+      Q st' := by rfl
868+
869+attribute [irreducible] ValidHoareTriple
870+
871+-- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing triples back
872+
873+-- This delaborator works only with `Com` from Imp.
874+
875+namespace Assertion.Delab
876+open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
877+@[delab app.HasTriple.Triple]
878+def delabTriple : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
879+  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``HasTriple.Triple 5
880+  guard <| (← getExpr).getArg! 0 == mkConst ``Com
881+  let P ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssn
882+  let c ← withNaryArg 3 delabComInner
883+  let Q ← withNaryArg 4 delabAssn
884+  ``({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }})
885+
886+end Assertion.Delab
887+
888+-- END DETAILS
889+
890+-- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
891+--     Is it possible to add a line break after the `Y := Y`?
892+
893+-- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_post_true ⭐
894+
895+-- Prove that if `Q` holds in every state, then any triple with `Q` as its
896+-- postcondition is valid.
897+
898+theorem hoare_post_true {P Q : Assertion} {c : Com} (h : ∀ st, Q st) :
899+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
900+  all_goals
901+    rw [validHoareTriple_def]
902+    intro st st' hc hpre
903+    exact h st'
904+
905+-- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_pre_false ⭐
906+
907+-- Prove that if `P` holds in no state, then any triple with `P` as its
908+-- precondition is valid.
909+
910+theorem hoare_pre_false {P Q : Assertion} {c : Com} (h : ∀ st, ¬ (P st)) :
911+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
912+  all_goals
913+    rw [validHoareTriple_def]
914+    intro st st' hc hpre
915+    specialize h st
916+    contradiction
917+
918+-- ## Proof Rules
919+
920+-- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
921+-- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
922+-- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
923+-- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
924+-- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
925+-- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
926+-- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
927+-- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
928+-- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
929+
930+-- ### Skip
931+
932+-- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
933+
934+--   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
935+--   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
936+
937+theorem hoare_skip {P : Assertion} :
938+    {{ P }} skip {{ P }} := by
939+  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
940+  intro st st' h hpre
941+  inversion h
942+  exact hpre
943+
944+-- ### Sequencing
945+
946+-- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
947+-- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
948+-- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
949+-- where `R` holds:
950+
951+--    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
952+--    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
953+--   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
954+--   {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
955+
956+theorem hoare_seq {P Q R : Assertion} {c1 c2 : Com}
957+    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
958+    {{ P }} ~c1; ~c2 {{ R }} := by
959+  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
960+  intro st st' h hpre
961+  inversion h with
962+  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
963+    rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h1 h2
964+    exact h1 hc2 (h2 hc1 hpre)
965+
966+-- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
967+-- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
968+-- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
969+-- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
970+-- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
971+-- through commands until we reach the beginning.
972+
973+-- ### Assignment
974+
975+-- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
976+-- rules. Here's how it works.
977+
978+-- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
979+
980+--   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
981+
982+-- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
983+-- could the precondition be?
984+
985+-- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
986+-- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
987+
988+--   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
989+
990+-- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
991+-- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
992+-- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
993+-- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
994+-- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
995+
996+-- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
997+
998+--   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
999+
1000+-- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
1001+-- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
1002+
1003+--   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
1004+
1005+-- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
1006+-- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
1007+-- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
1008+-- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
1009+-- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
1010+-- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
1011+-- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
1012+
1013+-- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
1014+-- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
1015+-- expression `a`:
1016+
1017+--   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
1018+
1019+-- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
1020+-- replaced by `a`.
1021+
1022+-- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
1023+-- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
1024+
1025+-- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
1026+
1027+--   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
1028+
1029+-- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
1030+-- terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
1031+-- start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted
1032+-- for every occurrence of `X`.
1033+
1034+-- To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it proceeds
1035+-- from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes good sense to
1036+-- go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is more important,
1037+-- because it characterizes what will be true after running the code.
1038+
1039+-- Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment rule.
1040+-- We'll do that later in some exercises.
1041+
1042+-- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
1043+
1044+--   {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
1045+--     X := X + 1
1046+--   {{ X ≤ 5 }}
1047+
1048+--   {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
1049+--     X := 3
1050+--   {{ X = 3 }}
1051+
1052+--   {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
1053+--     X := 3
1054+--   {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
1055+
1056+-- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of "substituting an
1057+-- expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which we refer to as
1058+-- assertion substitution, or `Assertion.subst`.
1059+
1060+-- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
1061+-- expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just the
1062+-- same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
1063+
1064+-- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions for
1065+-- Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends). The
1066+-- difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
1067+-- directly "edit" its text.
1068+
1069+-- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
1070+-- state, defined as follows:
1071+
1072+def Assertion.subst (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
1073+  fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
1074+
1075+-- Note to developers (One An @meluge, before next release):

1080+/-- Assertion substitution, written inside the braces: `{{ (P) [X ↦ a] }}`.
1081+The substituted assertion is re-read with the same notation, so Imp
1082+variables in it mean state lookups as usual; a named assertion is passed
1083+through directly. -/
1084+scoped syntax:max term:arg " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
1085+
1086+macro_rules
1087+  | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a:imp_aexp])) =>
1088+    match P with
1089+    | `($_:ident) => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) $P $st)
1090+    | _ => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $P }}) $st)
1091+
1092+theorem subst_def {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} {P : Assertion} :
1093+    Assertion.subst x a P = fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st) := by rfl
1094+
1095+@[simp]
1096+theorem subst_apply {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} {P : Assertion} {st : State} :
1097+    Assertion.subst x a P st ↔ P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st) := by rfl
1098+
1099+end Assertion

1134+-- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` -- that
1135+-- behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the variable `X`
1136+-- in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the expression `a`.
1137+
1138+-- To see how this works in more detail, let's calculate what happens with a
1139+-- couple of examples. First, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3]` -- that is,
1140+-- more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
1141+
1142+--   fun st =>
1143+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1144+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st 3 ; st),
1145+
1146+-- which simplifies to
1147+
1148+--   fun st =>
1149+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1150+--     (X →ₜ 3 ; st)
1151+
1152+-- and further simplifies to
1153+
1154+--   fun st =>
1155+--     ((X →ₜ 3 ; st)[X]) ≤ 5
1156+
1157+-- and finally to
1158+
1159+--   fun st =>
1160+--     3 ≤ 5.
1161+
1162+-- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `3` is less than or equal to `5` (as
1163+-- expected).
1164+
1165+-- For a more interesting example, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦
1166+-- X + 1]`.
1167+-- Formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
1168+
1169+--   fun st =>
1170+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1171+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st),
1172+
1173+-- which simplifies to
1174+
1175+--   fun st =>
1176+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st)[X] ≤ 5
1177+
1178+-- and further simplifies to
1179+
1180+--   fun st =>
1181+--     (Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 })) ≤ 5.
1182+
1183+-- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `X + 1` is at most `5`.
1184+
